78: The fish is calculated, not assumed. The calculator in the kit starts from the price you pay and the yield you get. With its default values, the usable cost per lb comes out at $11.28 for a whole farmed salmon, $23.92 for a salmon fillet bought clean and $25.48 for yellowfin tuna saku, and breaking down a whole salmon pays off only while your cleaning cost stays below about $12.65 per usable lb, the gap between the whole fish and the fillet. These are default values, a kit estimate you can edit: management blogs talk about 45% to 60% usable from a whole salmon, without a technical source. Clean and weigh three salmon, enter your yield on the "Fish Yield" tab and the calculator tells you how much cleaning cost still makes buying whole worthwhile. Costing works the same way. The "Costing" tab gives the food cost by piece: about 23% for a salmon nigiri, 12% for a California roll, 39% for a spicy tuna roll and 25% for a 24-piece party platter, and about 24% for the weighted menu. They are estimates that you measure with your own supplier, and the spicy tuna roll is the piece to watch.
79: Equipment is bought with a price and a source. The refrigerated sushi case of the case costs {{inv_vitrina}}; as a reference, a 71 in. Hoshizaki lists at $4,045 and a 60 in. countertop unit at $739. The two commercial gas rice cookers and the rice warmers come to {{inv_arroceras}}. The freezer holding -4 °F with a temperature logger costs {{inv_congelador}}, and the logger matters, because parasite destruction is documented. The hot kitchen, with the tempura fryer, the range and the griddle, is {{inv_cocina}}. The Type I hood with UL 300 fire suppression and makeup air costs {{inv_campana}}, the walk-in {{inv_camara}} and the reach-in fish refrigerators at 32-34 °F, prep tables, sake cooler and ice machine {{inv_frio}}. Plumbing, grease interceptor and gas lines are {{inv_fontaneria}}. The hood and the duct are the most delicate item of the space: get quotes before you sign the lease, and ask the mechanical inspector whether the gas rice cookers go under the hood.
80: Rice is measured too. With the kit's default values, 1 lb of raw rice gives about 2.41 lb of sushi rice, or about 51 nigiri, and for 115 covers the case cooks about 15 lb of raw rice a day. Rice is cheap: Calrose in a 50 lb bag runs about $1.04 per lb according to WebstaurantStore, and nori about $0.31 a sheet. The cost is in the fish and in the sushi chef's hands. So weigh ten slices of neta and ten balls of shari from each person at the bar. Neta and rice that weigh too much are food cost that never shows up in the costing. Every slice counts: the margin is in the rolls and the price is in the fish, so cut per service and never fill the sushi case just in case. The target is shrink of 5% or less of the fish you buy.
81: Food safety goes inside the operation, not beside it. Fish follows a route: receiving, cold storage, cleaning in its own zone and cutting at the bar. Hold it at 41 °F or below in the walk-in and the sushi case, keep the fish for service in a reach-in at 32-34 °F, and thaw it under refrigeration. Take the temperature of every delivery. Tuna, yellowtail and mackerel arrive at 40 °F or below or they go back, because histamine is not destroyed by freezing or by cooking. Keep the parasite destruction records by lot. Time-stamp every batch of sushi rice, or, if you run a variance, measure its pH with a calibrated meter and log it. The "Phase 3 - Raw Fish & Health" tab of the Sushi Restaurant Startup Checklist walks you through these logs. Use color-coded boards and separate knives for raw fish.
82: The case opens Tuesday through Sunday, 11:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. and 5:00 to 9:30 p.m., until 10:00 p.m. on Friday and Saturday. Production (the day's sushi rice, cutting the saku blocks and the sauces) is done before opening, so the head sushi chef and the line cook start at 8:30 a.m., three hours before the doors open. You need two fish suppliers with their paperwork, supplier letters or farmed-fish statements, and one for sushi rice, nori and sauces with specification sheets. Prices move with the season and the catch, so keep a second quote on hand. Utilities average {{suministros_mes}} a month, because the gas kitchen and the refrigeration run all day. Maintenance covers the semiannual hood cleaning, the refrigeration, the freezer that has to keep holding -4 °F and the rice cookers.
85: The team of the case is short, with seven rows on the "Staffing" tab. You are the owner and the general manager: you run the business, approve the menu and the food safety plan, and your pay is set below what a manager would earn, so think of an owner's draw in addition from net profit. The head sushi chef is a hire: buys, breaks down and cuts the fish, runs the bar at the busy service and signs the menu. With them are a sushi chef, who makes the sushi rice, the rolls and the marketplace platters and covers the bar when the head sushi chef is off, and a part-time sushi chef for dinners and weekends. A kitchen line cook handles the tempura, gyoza and rice. Four part-time servers also host and pack to-go orders, and one person handles dish and prep. Everyone is paid at least $15 an hour, and tips go on top of pay.
86: With relief for vacations and days off, the table adds up to {{plantilla_puestos}} people, equal to {{plantilla_jornadas_xl}} full-time equivalents, and costs {{personal_a1}} in year 1 including employer payroll taxes of {{cargas_pct}}, or {{personal_pct}} of sales. It is the biggest expense of the business, above goods and rent. Hours coverage is {{cobertura_horas}}. But the annual schedule hides a detail: on Friday and Saturday nights you need more people, with two at the sushi bar, one on the hot line, servers on the floor and someone packing to-go orders. Put it in the shift schedule. Staff grows with people, not with a percentage.
87: Pay every employee at least the highest of the federal minimum wage ($7.25 an hour, according to the Department of Labor, or {{salario_minimo_federal}} a year for a full-time employee at {{horas_semana}} hours a week), your state's and your city's, and remember that many are well above it. The case budgets at least $15 an hour and does not model a tip credit. The servers' tips belong to the servers and the team, as your state allows; the owner and the managers never keep tips. Hourly employees get overtime above 40 hours a week under the FLSA. Give every hire an offer letter, complete Form I-9 and Form W-4 on day one, and keep accurate time records in the POS. Your accountant or payroll provider confirms which rules apply to you.
88: The head sushi chef is the hard hire. Indeed puts the average sushi chef pay at $20.72 an hour in June 2026, within a range of $14.48 to $29.64, and a head sushi chef is paid above that. Hire this person before the build-out and ask for an opinion on the bar and the refrigeration. And think about the single-chef risk: it is not a saving, it is a risk, because if the only person who can run the bar is out, the bar does not open. Never replace payroll staff with 1099 contractors who work your schedule under your direction. That is misclassification, and the IRS, the Department of Labor and your state can all come after you for back taxes and penalties.
89: If you ever want your own delivery driver, in most states that person has to be a W-2 employee, and you will need hired and non-owned auto insurance. That is why the case has no in-house delivery: marketplace orders are delivered by the marketplace itself, and the weekend servers are for the floor and for packing to-go orders. Before putting a driver on the payroll, do the math: it is a fixed cost, while the marketplace charges its commission of {{comision_pct}} only when you sell.
90: Train the team before you open. Food handler cards are required in many states, and the Food Code asks for a Certified Food Protection Manager on site (2-102.12). With raw fish the training has to cover parasite destruction records, sushi case temperatures, the time control or pH log for the rice, the nine major allergens and cross-contact. The bar needs its own training in cutting and in the ounces of neta and shari. Separately, workplace safety covers cuts from the bar knives, burns from the fryer and the griddle, the cold of the freezer and heavy lifting.
93: To open you need {{inversion_total}}. That is {{capex}} for build-out ({{inv_obra}}), sushi bar, refrigeration, hood, equipment and opening, which includes the security deposit and {{meses_alquiler_previo}} months of rent paid before opening, plus {{fondo_maniobra}} of working capital. The cash needed at opening comes to {{necesidad_caja}}. The financing is {{fondos_propios}} of your own money and a {{prestamo}} SBA 7(a) loan at {{tipo_prestamo}} over {{plazo_prestamo}} years, with no interest-only period and an annual payment of {{cuota_anual}}. Sales tax is collected from guests, so it never enters the investment.
94: The three-year profit and loss projects revenue, excluding sales tax, of {{ventas_a1}}, {{ventas_a2}} and {{ventas_a3}}. Gross margin in year 1 is {{margen_bruto_pct}}, after all the variable costs: cost of goods ({{cogs_pct_xl}} of sales), disposables, delivery marketplace fees, card processing and contingency. Labor adds up to {{personal_a1}}, rent to {{ocupacion_anual}} ({{ocupacion_pct}} of sales) and marketing to {{marketing_anual}}. EBITDA, earnings before depreciation, interest and taxes, is {{ebitda_a1}}, or {{ebitda_pct_a1}} of sales. Net profit is {{resultado_neto_a1}}, {{resultado_neto_a2}} and {{resultado_neto_a3}}; the net margin in year 1 is {{margen_neto_a1}}, after an effective income tax rate of {{impuesto_beneficios}}. The example applies it as if the business paid corporate income tax (an LLC can elect it); as a pass-through, set the rate to 0 on "0. Assumptions" and budget your personal tax, and confirm with your CPA. To be honest about food cost: the plan uses {{food_cost_comida}} on food, the real usage of the whole menu with case shrink, trim you do not reuse, rice thrown out, staff meals and comps. The theoretical costing of the calculator comes out at about 24% for the weighted menu, and the gap is what is lost between the recipe and the register. Consulting blogs put sushi food cost at 30% to 40%.
95: The growth is the one the Excel makes: covers rise {{crecimiento_a2}} in year 2 and {{crecimiento_a3}} in year 3, from {{clientes_dia}} to {{clientes_a2}} and {{clientes_a3}} a day, at the same average check of {{ticket}} excluding sales tax. The sales mix is {{comida_pct}} food and {{bebida_pct}} beverage, and beer, sake and wine make up most of the beverage line. The other variable costs are disposables of {{consumibles_pct}} of sales, card fees of {{tarjeta_pct}}, and the marketplace, with {{plataforma_pct}} of sales at a commission of {{comision_pct}}. Together all variable costs come to {{costes_variables_pct}} of sales, and prime cost, goods plus labor, to {{prime_cost_pct}}. Sales tax is not revenue: the example uses {{sales_tax}}, a single rate, and some states tax to-go food differently, so check yours.
96: Accounting break-even is {{equilibrio_clientes_dia}} covers a day, or {{equilibrio_ventas}} a year in revenue. Cash break-even (loan payments in, depreciation out) is {{equilibrio_caja_clientes_dia}} covers a day, or {{equilibrio_caja_ventas}}, and leaves a margin of safety of {{holgura_caja_pct}} over the plan. The cash figure is the one to watch, because it is the one that pays the bank. The case has no interest-only period, so the margin is the same from year 1, but if you negotiate one it will look better until principal payments start: check the later years in the workbook before you celebrate. The {{clientes_dia}} covers a day on {{aforo}} seats imply {{rotaciones_dia}} seat turns a day, but covers include take-out and delivery orders that never sit at a table.
97: The cash flow numbers the months from 1 to 12, and Month 1 is January, in calendar order. The ramp-up starts at three-quarters of cruising speed and reaches it in four months, in April, which is why working capital counts. The lowest cash balance, {{saldo_minimo}}, is the one in Month {{mes_saldo_minimo}}, January, and the year ends in December, the peak. Sales tax is remitted on the schedule your state assigns, and the loan payment goes out every month. If you open in a different month, rotate the seasonality row of the Excel.
98: The minimum DSCR is {{dscr_min}}: the business covers its debt with room to spare. Payback before debt comes from the cash flow: {{payback}} with the working capital reserve counted in the investment, and {{payback_capex}} on startup costs alone. Recovery depends on the bar delivering every day: this is a craft business, not an annuity. If the numbers do not work, the lever is the menu price, never more debt.
99: The pessimistic scenario is a weak year: {{pesimista_clientes}} covers a day at an average check of {{pesimista_ticket}} over {{pesimista_dias}} days gives sales of {{pesimista_ventas}} and a pre-tax loss of {{pesimista_perdida}}. In the optimistic one, {{optimista_clientes}} covers at {{optimista_ticket}} over {{optimista_dias}} days give sales of {{optimista_ventas}} and a pre-tax result of {{optimista_resultado}}. Every point of food cost on food sales takes about 1% of food sales straight out of profit, and the price of salmon and tuna is volatile, so measure your real usage (food purchases divided by food sales for the month) in the first quarter and change the cell. The Excel rules, and if you change a green cell, this document stays behind.
102: Most owners open as an LLC, which you file with your state, and many add an operating agreement; talk to your CPA about LLC versus S corp taxation. Then get an EIN from the IRS and register for a sales tax permit with your state. In the US, requirements stack in layers: federal, state, county and city, and each one has its own forms. Apply for the city or county business license and, before you sign anything, run a zoning check on the exact address for restaurant use and the hood. Submit your plans for plan review with the health department (Food Code 8-201.11 asks for plans before construction or remodeling), then get your building permit and, at the end, the certificate of occupancy, with the fire marshal's sign-off. The workbook uses an example sales tax of {{sales_tax}}, a single rate; some states tax to-go food differently, so check yours.
103: Fire and the hood come first. A Type I hood with UL 300 fire suppression and makeup air goes over the tempura fryer, the range and the griddle, and the hood is cleaned twice a year (NFPA 96). Ask the mechanical inspector whether the gas rice cookers go under the hood, and plan for a grease interceptor. Before the health permit you will have a pre-opening inspection, with the walk-in, the reach-in fish refrigerators and the freezer with its logger in place. The Food Code asks for a Certified Food Protection Manager on site (2-102.12), and many states also require food handler cards for the rest of the team. Used fryer oil goes to a licensed grease hauler.
104: Raw fish is the sensitive point. Under the FDA Food Code 2022 (3-402.11; each state adopts its own edition), fish served raw or undercooked must be frozen first: at -4 °F (-20 °C) or below for 7 days (168 hours), or at -31 °F until solid and held for 15 hours, or at -31 °F until solid and then held at -4 °F or below for the 24-hour option. Besides bivalves and roe removed from the skein and rinsed, two groups are exempt: tuna of the Thunnus species (yellowfin, bigeye, bluefin, albacore) and farmed fish fed pellet feed, such as salmon; the farmed fish need a written statement from the supplier or the farmer, and the kit also files the tuna invoice that names the species. Freezing records are kept 90 days (3-402.12). The kit's SOP is to buy fish already treated, with the supplier letter on file, and to use the -4 °F freezer for that stock. Farmed hamachi, mackerel (saba), squid and wild fish need a supplier letter or your own freezing with records. "Sushi-grade" has no legal definition, so do not promise it. Tuna, yellowtail and mackerel carry histamine: receive them at 40 °F or below or reject them (FDA Fish and Fishery Products Hazards and Controls Guidance).
105: Cooked sushi rice is a TCS food (B. cereus), and the Food Code gives you two routes. The first is time as a public health control (TPHC, 3-501.19): up to 4 hours without temperature control, with the time stamped on every batch and a written procedure available to the inspector, and at 4 hours the rice is discarded, not chilled or reheated. This is the default in the case. The second is a variance with a HACCP plan for acidified rice (3-502.11(C)); the annex of the Code gives an example critical limit of pH below 4.2, but each county sets its own, with a calibrated pH meter and a log for every batch. The kit sets no legal pH: decide TPHC or variance with your health department in writing before opening. The consumer advisory (3-603.11) has two parts, a disclosure (an asterisk or description on every raw dish) and a reminder ("Consuming raw or undercooked ... seafood ... may increase your risk of foodborne illness"), and it goes on the menu, the website and your marketplace listings.
106: The nine major allergens are fish, crustacean shellfish, milk, eggs, peanuts, tree nuts, wheat, soy and sesame, which was added in 2023 under the FASTER Act. In sushi, fish and crustacean shellfish (shrimp, crab) are on the menu itself. Soy and wheat are in soy sauce (tamari only if the label says so), sesame is in seeds and oil, egg is in spicy mayo, tamago and tempura batter, milk is in the cream cheese, and wheat is in tempura and panko. Imitation crab often contains wheat starch and egg white, so go by the label. Mollusks and mustard are not major allergens in the United States, though they are in the UK. Do not promise "gluten-free" (21 CFR 101.91): soy sauce and tempura contain wheat and the fryer is shared. Make an allergen matrix by dish before opening and review it whenever you change a supplier or a sauce.
107: The beer and wine license comes from a state agency plus local approval. Sake usually goes under the wine license, so ask your state's alcohol beverage control agency. Apply early and never count on it. Liquor liability goes in your insurance, together with general liability, product liability for raw fish, property and workers' comp, which come to {{seguros_anual}} a year in the case. Staff are W-2 employees paid by the hour, never 1099 for sushi chefs or servers, with Form I-9 and Form W-4 on day one. Tips belong to the team; the managers and the owner never keep tips. Add music licenses (ASCAP, BMI and SESAC) and check local packaging ordinances, because some cities ban polystyrene.
108: Selling sushi from your home kitchen is another matter. There is no federal rule, and state cottage food laws do not cover raw fish or cooked rice, both TCS foods, so this plan assumes a permitted restaurant, and you should check your state before you try anything else. This section lists what we can state with confidence; for everything else, check with your accountant, your city or the health inspector before you decide. A note for UK readers: register your food business with your local council at least 28 days before you open and expect a Food Hygiene Rating of 0 to 5 (FHIS in Scotland). Fish to be eaten raw must be frozen at -4 °F (-20 °C) for 24 hours or at -31 °F (-35 °C) for 15 hours, with no exemption for tuna (retained Regulation 853/2004; check with your council). VAT is 20% on dine-in and hot food, while cold take-away sushi is usually zero-rated (check HMRC VAT Notice 709/1). There are 14 allergens to declare, including molluscs, mustard, celery, sulphites and lupin, and a premises licence plus a personal licence if you sell alcohol.
111: The conclusion is that a neighborhood sushi restaurant of this size is viable, but demanding. With {{clientes_dia}} covers a day at {{ticket}} per cover, excluding sales tax, the first year leaves a net profit of {{resultado_neto_a1}} and a margin of safety of {{holgura_caja_pct}} over cash break-even. The minimum DSCR is {{dscr_min}}, the lowest cash balance is {{saldo_minimo}} in January and payback before debt is {{payback}} with the working capital reserve counted. It is a craft business, sustained by a full bar every day, and it is not for going in with thin capital.
112: These are the thirteen mistakes of a sushi restaurant and how to avoid them. The first is opening without a head sushi chef, or with only one: hire before the build-out and train a second person early, because if the bar has no one, it does not open. The second is assuming that fresh salmon needs no paperwork: farmed salmon needs the supplier's written statement, and wild fish and non-exempt species need freezing under 3-402.11 with records. The third is a freezer that does not hold -4 °F, or one with no logger, and records that are not kept for 90 days.
113: The fourth is leaving sushi rice out without a time stamp and a written TPHC procedure, or a variance, and not discarding it at 4 hours. The fifth is the marketplace with no ceiling: the commission and the card fees eat the margin, and rolls and platters travel well but tempura does not, which is why the ceiling of the plan is {{plataforma_pct}} of sales. The sixth is a long menu that fills the sushi case with neta that you end up throwing out: better short, with the case sized to the service.
114: The seventh is pricing a platter without costing it by channel: the same 24-piece platter leaves about a fifth less margin when it goes out through a marketplace than when it is sold dine-in ($24.83 against $31.60 with the calculator's defaults). The eighth is depending on one fish supplier: two, with their paperwork, are the insurance of the bar. The ninth is incomplete allergens: sesame, soy and wheat are in the sauces, the tempura and the imitation crab, as well as the fish itself. A matrix by dish, made before opening and reviewed whenever you change a supplier or a sauce, avoids the scare.
115: The tenth is leaving the consumer advisory off the menu, the website or the marketplace listings. The eleventh is receiving tuna, yellowtail or mackerel above 40 °F without a receiving log: histamine does not go away with freezing or cooking. The twelfth is promising "gluten-free" with soy sauce, tempura and a shared fryer: it is not promised. And the thirteenth is copying the figures of a franchise or of a different-size space for your case: they are good for comparing, not for budgeting. Almost all of these mistakes have their task in the checklist, set in the order in which it makes sense to do it.
116: The action plan has six phases and 80 tasks in the checklist that comes with the kit. "Phase 1 - Business Setup" has 12 tasks. "Phase 2 - Hood & Permits" has 15. "Phase 3 - Raw Fish & Health" has 14. "Phase 4 - Staff & Allergens" has 13. "Phase 5 - Menu, Brand, Delivery" has 13. And "Phase 6 - Opening & 90 Days" has 13. Follow the order: the zoning check and the fire marshal's answer on the hood and the duct come before you sign the lease, the beer and wine license application goes in as soon as you do, your health department's answer on TPHC or a variance for the rice comes in writing before you open, and the head sushi chef is hired before the build-out. Check off each task when you close it, and if one slips, see what depends on it before you move the opening date.
117: The next step is to fill in the Excel with your own numbers: your real rent, your average check, your covers, your loan, your staff and your opening calendar. Change only the green cells; this document reflects the example case, and yours is set by your spreadsheet. Then, with the Sushi Fish, Rice & Costing Calculator, measure the yield of your salmon and the real ounces of neta and shari, and in the first quarter compare your actual food cost with the {{food_cost_comida}} in the plan. For the logs of rice time, freezing and the sushi case, use the "Phase 3 - Raw Fish & Health" tab of the Sushi Restaurant Startup Checklist. With your own data in front of you, come back to this section and check what is left in cash in years 2 and 3 if the year turns out like the pessimistic scenario.
